articles.title: A might-is-right world
articles.content: THE world is passing through one of the most volatile periods in modern history. It is more unstable today than at any time since the end of the Cold War. The international system is fragmenting with rising big-power tensions. The old order with whatever rules it had is gone. Power shifts continue to reshape the international landscape, marking the advent of a multipolar era. The disregard for international law and norms by big and regional powers has left countries having to navigate a rule-less terrain at a time of great uncertainty. Hard power has made a comeback. Powerful countries and regional powers are using military force or other coercive instruments to try to bend other states to their will. The threat or the use of force has become an option of first and not last resort, and the means to prevail over others. These actions defy international law and global norms but continue with impunity. Diplomacy only happens after missiles have been fired. Conflicts proliferate across the world — two major wars, between theUS-Israel and Iranand between Ukraine and Russia as well as Israel’s genocidal war in Gaza and military actions against its neighbours. There are a record number of conflicts today. A study by a Swedish university has counted the highest number of conflicts between states in 2025 since World War II. There are 65 active conflicts according to its data for last year. The risk of a global conflagration is also heightening. Can this push the world to the brink of a third world war? A new book seeks to answer this frequently raised question. War is Interested in You: The Breakdown of International Order and the Threat of World War Three by distinguished British columnist Gideon Rachman is an insightful book on a subject that is especially relevant today. He borrows the book’s title from Trotsky: “You may not be interested in war, but war is interested in you” — meaning war will come whether anyone wants it or is thinking about it. Rachman identifies three fundamental reasons for the surge in conflicts and breakdown of international order. The first is the shifting global balance of power which is challenging US dominance. The second is the rise of what he calls ‘strongmen leaders’ who regard war as a necessary and legitimate tool to achieve their ends. The third is a consequence of the first two; as these trends take hold international rules and law are breaking down. “A law-governed world is giving way to a might-makes-right world,” he writes. In explaining these causal factors, Rachman argues that the relative decline of the Western alliance and America’s retrenchment from its global role created an “opening” for “revisionist” powers dissatisfied with the present world order to take more risks. He cites Russia’s invasion of Ukraine and China’s more aggressive posture on Taiwan as cases in point. Trump’s use of military force against Iran, in defiance of international law and ignoring the views of its allies, has further contributed to the collapse of global order. Can distinct regional conflicts merge to push the world to the brink of a third world war? Greater international insecurity also stems from the emergence of a new generation of self-styled strongman leaders — Putin, Trump, Netanyahu — who deride the idea of a rules-based international order. Their acceptance of territorial annexation and belief in ‘might-makes-right’ has heightened the risk of international conflict. Rachman suggests that both Trump and Putin subscribe to the “spheres of influence” theory, which they see as a more reliable guarantor of peace and stability than a rules-based order. The starkest expression of this, he asserts, is Trump’s revival of the Monroe doctrine for the Western Hemisphere. In what Rachman characterises as a “might is right” world, growing global insecurity is driving up defence spending. Global rules and international institutions are being upended by strongman leaders, increasing the risk of more wars. While acts of war are the most dramatic examples of the breakdown of the rules-based order, Rachman argues that international institutions are crumbling in other ways too. Trump’s trade war and protectionist policies are, for example, accelerating this erosion. Rachman examines today’s major wars and argues that while they have been distinct regional conflicts, they intersect at various points. But as these separate conflicts escalate, they risk eventually merging. His concept of an ‘axis of adversaries’ of the West or ‘axis of upheaval’ challenging the US-led world order greatly exaggerates the degree of cooperation between Russia, China, North Korea, and Iran whose interests are hardly identical. They may all want an end to US hegemony but that doesn’t make them partners in an alliance acting in unison. The argument does not stand up to scrutiny. Rachman is unable to convincingly establish the “practical and ideological” links he posits between them. In fact, he himself acknowledges the limits of the Russian-Chinese partnership and strains among the four countries. To the question of whether a conflict-ridden world is heading towards a global conflagration, Rachman’s answer is carefully qualified. A world war, he argues, would have two defining characteristics. One, the world’s major powers would have to be in direct conflict as they were in the First and Second World Wars. Two, the conflict would have to span continents. These conditions do not obtain today but they cannot be ruled out in the future.He sees a direct conflict between the US and China as the greatest risk. Rachman devotes a chapter to last year’sconflict between India and Pakistan. It adds little to what has already been written about the military confrontation between the two nuclear neighbours. He sees the four-day conflict in May 2025 as a serious setback to India’s ambitions and efforts to de-hyphenate from Pakistan. Among the lessons he draws from this episode is that “the risks of a very dangerous conflict in South Asia get too little attention compared to other global trouble spots”. He argues that the risk of future conflicts is heightened by the fact that both countries deployed increasingly sophisticated weapons during the crisis. This is an intelligent book well worth reading for its sharp perspectives on war and peace even if one might disagree with some of the author’s assertions. The writer is a former ambassador to the US, UK and UN.
articles.author: Maleeha Lodhi

articles.title: Medicating a broken system
articles.content: THE psychiatric profession faces a fundamental question: are we treating people’s distress as a problem located inside their minds when much of what troubles them lies outside, in the conditions of their lives? The question has particular urgency in Pakistan, where a recent national survey of more than 17,000 individuals showed that one in three adults suffers from some sort of diagnosable mental disorder. What is leading to this mental health crisis in Pakistan? The answer may lie in understanding people’s circumstances rather than assigning diagnoses. Unfortunately, we have become so preoccupied with diagnosing and treating individuals that we have lost sight of the social conditions that make them ill. What does it mean to treat the anxiety of someone whose future is insecure or offer counselling to a man who cannot provide for his family? How far can psychological therapy help a woman who is in constant fear due to unabated domestic violence? Treatment may offer some relief, at least temporarily, but if the circumstances remain unchanged, we risk helping the person endure a problem that society continues to create — and ignore. This is the central limitation of an individualised approach to mental health: it turns a social problem into a personal responsibility. Pakistan’s mental health discourse focuses on ‘raising awareness, reducing stigma, increasing access to psychological support, early identification, and referral to specialist services’. While these are important, they can become politically convenient substitutes for confronting the structural determinants of psychological distress. Awareness campaigns do not create jobs. Teaching resilience through mental health apps does not increase household incomes. Screening programmes do not stop domestic violence or child sexual abuse. Counselling cannot substitute for social protection, affordable education and health, or protection against violence. This is the contradiction in Pakistan’s policies: awareness without accountability. This becomes particularly stark when the government acknowledges mental health as a public health priority but does nothing to address the economic and social factors that people face daily. We need to move beyond the narrow thinking that mental health improves when people become more aware of mental illness and more willing to seek treatment. We must also ask why so many people are exposed to toxic conditions that threaten their well-being in the first place. Improving mental health requires more than treating the consequences of social and economic failure. Locating distress primarily within individuals obscures questions of power and responsibility. When social adversity is translated into individual diagnoses, ignoring the person’s context, he/she becomes the site of intervention while institutions and governments escape scrutiny. When we teach people resilience we reinforce that the central task is to help people withstand adversity rather than reduce the adversity itself. In Pakistan, marked by profound inequalities, it turns psychiatry, however unintentionally, into an instrument of adaptation to injustice. Instead, we should ask: what has happened to this person, and what continues to make their life difficult? Mental health assessments should explore not only symptoms and psychiatric history but also employment, debt, housing, family relationships, violence, etc. It is important to understand the person’s own explanation of their distress rather than assuming that a diagnostic label of ‘depression’ or ‘anxiety’ provides the complete account. This approach does not eliminate diagnosis or medication. Those experiencing severe symptoms should have access to evidence-based treatment. The distinction is between using biomedical interventions when indicated and treating the biomedical explanation as sufficient in every case. The approach also has important policy implications. Pakistan has a good record of developing policies but an extremely poor one for implementing them. There is no reason to be optimistic that the recently launched National Mental Health Policy will not meet the same fate. It is futile to talk about a mental health policy without integrating social determinants into planning and also having a clear strategy for their implementation. The federal and provincial governments must be held accountable for how they will do so. Mental health programmes must be evaluated against outcomes that matter in people’s lives, not simply symptom improvement. Mental health professionals and institutions must engage with the political and economic conditions shaping their patients’ lives. It requires them to recognise that suffering has social causes and that their professional obligations do not end at the clinic door. They must be willing to speak truth to power and not simply have their photographs taken with government officials and political leaders. Pakistan does not face a choice between treating mental illness and addressing poverty, inequality, or violence. It needs both. The mistake is investing in the former while neglecting the latter. A diagnosis is never a complete explanation, and an effective treatment plan must take into account people’s circumstances. How ethical is it to ask people to become more resilient to bear conditions that public policy could make less damaging or ask people to practise relaxation exercises while their livelihoods collapse, to cultivate optimism while their prospects disappear, or to develop coping skills while they remain exposed to violence? Such interventions may provide relief, but they cannot substitute for social justice. Pakistan’s mental health crisis cannot be addressed solely through more psychiatrists, better access to mental health services (which are poorly organised anyway), more prescriptions, more awareness campaigns, or more screening. These are necessary components of care, but they cannot compensate for policies that perpetuate insecurity and exclusion. Improving mental health requires more than treating the consequences of social and economic failure. It requires taking responsibility for the conditions that produce them. A society committed to mental well-being must do more than teach people how to endure their circumstances. It must also work to make those circumstances more bearable. The writer is professor emeritus of psychiatry at Aga Khan University.
articles.author: Murad Moosa Khan

articles.title: Pyramid of pain
articles.content: WHAT is the common thread in all these cases? In 2026, a 14-year-old girl in Pakistantortures and kills her pet cat, sending the pictures of the abuse to an unknown person for approval. In late 2024 in Stockholm, a 14-year-old boy walks up to a man in his 80s, stabs him repeatedly in the back and flees, taking nothing from his victim except blood. Another teenager in the same country tries to coerce a 13-year-old to take his own life and video-stream his suicide. In the US state of Oregon, a 16-year-old shoots and kills three students and a teacher at an elementary school before being shot dead. A year earlier, in the same state, a 14-year-old was arrested for planning a mass shooting/ suicide at a mall. In June 2026, a school shooting takes place in the Philippines where two suspects, aged 14 and 15,killedthree students and wounded 20 others. In all these cases, the driving force for this kind of torture, self-harm, murder, and suicide is a shadowy online group called 764 that is dedicated to the ‘gamification’ of violence, in which your online status rises in proportion to the harm you can do — to yourself or, preferably, to others. 764 takes its name from the first three digits of the zip code for Stephenville, Texas, the home of its founder Bradley Cadenhead, known online as Felix, who created this group in 2021 when he was 15. While he is now serving 80 years in a US prison after being convicted of possessing child sexual abuse material, his network not only survives, but is considered a tier-1 security threat in the US, alongside the likes of Al Qaeda and IS, and — as evidence of its transnational reach and decentralised nature — is also listed as a terrorist group in New Zealand and Canada, to name just two. But what sets 764 apart from ‘mainstream’ terrorist groups is its ideology, or lack thereof. There’s no political agenda, barring perhaps a shared hatred for humanity, a desire to dismantle morality as a whole, and to accelerate, as some of its adherents put it, the destruction of society. Defined by the FBI as “violent nihilistic extremism”, it promotes harm for the sake of harm; they are the engagement farmers of evil. The hunt for victims begins on social media pages frequented by young people or the chat servers of otherwise perfectly innocent games like Minecraft and Roblox, and then shifts onto Discord servers or Telegram. With a predator’s instinct, they target the young, the vulnerable, and as forensic psychologist Joni Johnston puts it, the “sad and the strange”. Once suitable targets are identified, a well-thought-out process of psychological manipulation, extortion, and coercion begins in which victims often turn into perpetrators who can then rise in the ranks depending on how many others they can coerce or blackmail into committing atrocities. The 764 group and the larger networks it is affiliated with even publish grooming and blackmail guides and digital scrapbooks (‘lorebooks’ in their parlance) of their exploits, not only gaining them further clout and respect in their twisted system of merit but also serving as ‘how-to’ guides for new recruits. The initial approach is cloaked in kindness; from there, it often turns into romantic overtures intended to gain the victim’s trust. Once compromising pictures of and personal information on the victim are obtained, they are used to blackmail the victims into acts like progressively harming themselves, their pets, or other human beings. Typical ‘tasks’ and ‘challenges’ entail cutting the 764 logo into one’s arm or writing the online nickname of one’s ‘controller’ in blood and then sending photographic evidence to the group. The deeper they get, the more they are threatened with exposure by the 764 group. Once control has been established, the victims are made to victimise others and commit serious crimes, much like a pyramid scheme of pain. In the US alone, 764 has been linked to at least five mass shootings. Its founder didn’t invent the grooming method he and his followers use; he borrowed it from already existing groups like CVLT and Greggy’s Cult, which specialised in coercing children to expose themselves sexually or harm themselves. Cadenhead had come across these groups when he was 10 and was sent real footage of people being tortured while on a Minecraft server. 764 is only one part of a much larger network known as ‘The Com’ which is short for ‘Community’, and shares this status with other accelerationist, neo-Nazi, and openly satanic sub-groups such as No Lives Matter, Satanic Front, and Maniacs Murder Club. In one sense, the rise of such groups is a sign of the depths to which society has sunk, where traditional morality is to be mocked and self-gratification is the greatest good. And in these murky deeps, there are sharks.
articles.author: Zarrar Khuhro

articles.title: Finance at COP31
articles.content: AS the world prepares for COP31, Pakistan has an opportunity to advance a pioneering climate finance agenda that connects the security of the Hindukush-Karakoram-Himalaya (HKH) with the survival of Small Island Developing States (SIDS). The case should be built on the premise that if the international community recognises the exceptional vulnerability of SIDS through dedicated allocations from the Fund for Responding to Loss and Damage (FRLD), it should extend comparable consideration to the cryosphere, whose accelerating degradation is a major driver of sea-level rise and a growing source of catastrophic losses across Asia. This should not be seen as a competition between vulnerable regions. It is a call for climate finance that addresses both the people exposed to climate impacts and the physical processes generating them. Sea-level rise that threatens the very existence of many island nations begins with the cryosphere. Therefore, an effective response must look beyond the coastline to the cryospheric changes driving the rising water. Two major contributors to global mean sea-level rise are the loss of land-based ice, particularly glaciers and ice sheets, and the thermal expansion of warming oceans. Melting sea ice, by contrast, contributes little directly to sea-level rise because it already floats. This distinction matters because the cryosphere is not a single, uniform system, but its land-based ice stores enormous quantities of freshwater that, when lost to the oceans, raise sea levels. At COP31, Pakistan should seek a ‘Cryosphere Declaration’. The policy implication is clear. Financing recovery after coastal flooding, erosion, and saltwater intrusion is essential, but investing in recovery without adequately addressing the drivers of those losses is economically short-sighted. The world must finance protection against sea-level rise while urgently reducing the emissions that accelerate ice loss. Protecting the cryosphere and maintaining the annual cyclical hydrology of melting and replenishment will reduce risks for both HKH countries and SIDS. Moreover, a cryospheric crisis in the HKH will have continental consequences. According to the International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development, the river basins originating here support some 1.9 billion people. This is a population whose water, food, energy, and economic security depend substantially on the health of the mountain cryosphere. The UN puts the combined population of SIDS at around 65 million. These populations are not directly equivalent measures of climate vulnerability, but the scale of downstream exposure makes a compelling case for comparable global attention and dedicated finance for the HKH cryosphere. The HKH’s threats also differ from those of the Arctic. Arctic ice loss is globally consequential, particularly through the contribution of Greenland’s ice sheet to sea-level rise, alongside wider effects on polar ecosystems and climate systems. The HKH, by contrast, combines extensive mountain glaciers, seasonal snow, thawing permafrost, and expanding glacial lakes with densely populated downstream river basins. Its cryosphere is both a water reservoir and a source of rapidly escalating hazards. The latest UNEP Emissions Gap Report 2026, released last month, warns that global temperatures are set to exceed 1.5 degrees Celsius above pre-industrial levels. Even the lowest overshoot pathway would require global greenhouse gas emissions to fall by 18 per cent by 2030, 45pc by 2035 and 69pc by 2040, relative to 2025 levels. Current national pledges fall far short of this trajectory, while current policies could lead to around 2.8°C of warming this century. This is precisely why climate finance must move beyond treating disasters solely as events to be compensated for after they occur, and connect mitigation and adaptation as part of a dedicated cryosphere funding connecting all three. The existing commitment to a 50pc allocation floor for least developed countries and SIDS during the Loss and Damage Fund’s start-up phase provides an important precedent for targeted support. At COP31, Pakistan should seek a ‘Cryosphere Declaration’ that recognises the HKH as a global climate-risk priority and establishes a pathway for dedicated cryosphere finance under FRLD, the Adaptation Fund and mitigation financing. The declaration should promote regional scientific cooperation, sustained observation networks and measurable action to reduce climate risks. Diplomacy in building alliances with SIDS and the Alliance of Small Island States, framing the proposal as a common campaign to finance both the sources of climate-related risks and the communities suffering their consequences, will prevent future losses for both SIDS and HKH countries.
articles.author: Aisha Khan

articles.title: Without consequence
articles.content: JOURNALISTS today face ever more sophisticated threats, while those who target them continue to walk free. From drone attacks to online harassment and legal intimidation, the methods of silencing reporters are multiplying, with little fear of punishment. This year’s International Day to End Impunity for Crimes against Journalists, observed today, carries the theme ‘Threats Evolve. Impunity Endures’. According to Unesco, 189 journalists were killed in 2024 and 2025, most of them in conflict zones. Yet justice remains elusive in the vast majority of cases. The global impunity rate has risen to 86pc, the first increase since Unesco began measuring it in 2012. This failure to punish those responsible sends a dangerous message: journalists can be attacked or killed without fear of consequence. Gaza shows what happens when those responsible are not held to account. The Committee to Protect Journalists recorded 129 journalists killed worldwide in 2025, with Israel responsible for two-thirds of the deaths. In August that year,Israeli strikeson Gaza’s Nasser Hospital killed 22 people, including five journalists. AnAPinvestigation published a year later found that nobody had been held accountable. For Palestinian journalists, who have been reporting a war largely closed to foreign media, the dangers are especially severe. Their deaths leave the outside world with fewer people able to document what is happening. Similarly, in Sudan and Ukraine, journalists risk their lives exposing the horrors of war, while those who target them often escape justice. Without independent investigations and punishment for those found responsible, promises to protect journalists will remain empty. Pakistan’s record is also deeply troubling. Freedom Network’s latestreportdocuments threats and assaults against journalists, along with 45 cases of legal action or threatened prosecution. The growing use of Peca against journalists investigating official wrongdoing is particularly worrying. Repeated summonses, seized devices and costly court battles are enough to silence a reporter even without a conviction. The human cost of this failure is evident in thecase of journalist Mudassar Mahmood Naru. Eight years after his disappearance, his son is growing up without a father and his family is still waiting for answers. The laws meant to protect journalists offer little comfort when the bodies responsible for enforcing them fail to act. In smaller towns, where reporters have fewer resources, intimidation often goes unreported. The state must ensure that attacks are properly investigated, protection bodies function and cybercrime laws are not used to punish legitimate reporting. A country where journalists fear telling the truth more than wrongdoers fear being exposed has its priorities wrong.
articles.author: Editorial

articles.title: Climate diagnosis
articles.content: THE Lancet Countdown’s latest findings should change how Pakistan thinks about illness as much as how it thinks about climate change. The report estimates that heat contributed to 710,000 deaths worldwide in 2023. In Pakistan, a patient arriving at a clinic with dehydration, kidney injury or breathing difficulties may be experiencing the effects of extreme weather without that connection ever entering the medical record. A child treated for diarrhoea after flooding, or an elderly person whose heart condition deteriorates during prolonged heat, becomes another isolated case rather than part of a wider pattern. The result is a dangerous knowledge gap. Without reliable information on where climate-related illnesses occur, who is most affected and how many lives are lost, health authorities cannot judge the scale of the problem. Climate change is already altering the demands placed on medicine; Pakistan’s healthcare planning has yet to catch up. This is where the warning from former health officials deserves closer attention. Rather than producing another catalogue of vulnerabilities, the government should begin with what hospitals and clinics can actually record, diagnose and treat. Provincial health departments could require major facilities to track heatstroke, dehydration, acute kidney injury and other conditions aggravated by extreme weather, with data reviewed alongside local temperature and rainfall trends. Primary-care staff need practical guidance for recognising heat illness early, especially among children, older people and patients taking medicines that affect hydration. Hospitals should examine whether their emergency departments can cope with seasonal surges, and whether essential treatment can continue when power or water supplies fail. None of this requires waiting for another international declaration. It requires health officials to treat climate exposure as a routine part of patient care. Public reporting would also reveal which districts lack the staff, equipment and referral arrangements to respond. Pakistan has spent years describing itself as vulnerable to climate change. The Lancet findings present a more immediate challenge: can its health system identify the people being harmed, offer them treatment and learn enough from their cases to prevent avoidable deaths?
articles.author: Editorial
